country.name: Argentina
country.tagline: Malbec at altitude: desert oases fed by Andean snowmelt, from the Tropic of Capricorn to the Patagonian wind.

stats.note: Vineyard: INV, all grape vines at 31 Dec 2024 (Malbec report 2025). Production: INV 2026 annual report, 9,700,421 hl (down 9.9% on 2025). Rank: OIV 2025, where Argentina made 10.8 mhl, 6th in the world.

country.overview:
Argentina makes wine in the desert. Almost every vineyard lies in the rain shadow of the Andes, in irrigated oases strung along rivers of snowmelt between the Tropic of Capricorn in Jujuy and 45°S in Chubut. Rainfall is often 200 mm a year or less, the sun shines on more than 300 days, and the only reason a vine can grow is a canal network whose oldest channels follow Huarpe and Inca irrigation. Height does the work that latitude does in Europe. Vineyards run from about 500 m on the eastern plains of Mendoza to 1,500 m in the Uco Valley and above 3,000 m in the Calchaquí valleys of Salta, among the highest commercial vineyards on Earth. Every 100 m of altitude costs roughly 0.6°C, so the higher sites keep acidity and freshness while the intense ultraviolet light thickens grape skins.

The vine came from Chile and Peru with Spanish priests and conquistadors in the 1550s: to Santiago del Estero in 1557, to Mendoza after its founding in 1561, to San Juan soon after. For three centuries the country drank wine from Criolla grapes, the Listán Prieto family that Chile calls País. The modern story begins in 1853, when Domingo Faustino Sarmiento's Quinta Normal in Mendoza, run by the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, brought French varieties including Malbec. The railway from Buenos Aires reached Mendoza in 1885, carrying Italian and Spanish immigrants west and their wine east, and by the early 20th century Argentina had one of the largest wine industries in the world, built on cheap table wine for a nation that drank about 90 litres a head in the 1970s.

That model collapsed in the 1980s, along with consumption, hyperinflation and much of the old Malbec vineyard. The rebirth of the 1990s came from looking outward: foreign capital and flying winemakers, drip irrigation, yield control, new oak, and above all a few producers who bet on altitude and on Malbec. Nicolás Catena planted the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary in 1992, when locals thought it was too cold to ripen anything. French investors arrived in the Uco Valley (Clos de los Siete, Cheval des Andes), and by the 2000s Argentine Malbec, plush, violet-scented and affordable, had become one of the wine world's great export stories.

Malbec is now the most planted grape in the country, 47,064 ha in 2024 according to INV, 23.5% of the national vineyard and present in 18 of 20 wine provinces. It is joined by Bonarda (Douce Noir of Savoie), Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, the pink-skinned Criolla Grande and Cereza that still fill boxes and demijohns, and Torrontés Riojano, the floral white born in Argentina from Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica. Phylloxera is present, but in a weak form held back by sandy soils and flood irrigation, so most vineyards remain ungrafted.

The frontier of the 2010s and 2020s is precision. Mendoza's Uco Valley has been carved into district IGs drawn on geology (Paraje Altamira, Los Chacayes, San Pablo, Pampa El Cepillo), producers map calcareous crusts and river stones parcel by parcel, and new IGs keep appearing in the high north, the Andean valleys of San Juan, Patagonia and even the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires. At the same time the domestic industry is shrinking: the 2026 harvest of 18.6 million quintals was among the lowest on record, wine output fell to 9.7 million hectolitres, and the national vineyard has lost tens of thousands of hectares in a decade. Argentines still drink more wine than anyone else in the Americas, about 21 litres per adult in 2025 according to the OIV, and wine has been the national drink by law since 2013.

history.title: First vines at Santiago del Estero
history.text: Vine cuttings from Chile are planted at Santiago del Estero, the oldest Spanish town in Argentina; tradition credits the priest Juan Cedrón (or Cidrón). The grape is the Criolla family, ancestor of Criolla Chica and cousin of Chile's País.

history.title: Mendoza is founded
history.text: Pedro del Castillo founds Mendoza on 2 March 1561. Spanish settlers extend the Huarpe irrigation canals, and vineyards spread through Cuyo; San Juan follows from 1562. Wine and aguardiente travel by cart and mule to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and the silver city of Potosí.

history.title: Jesuit estancias
history.text: Jesuit estancias around Córdoba, such as Caroya, make wine for their colleges until the order's expulsion in 1767; the estancias are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

history.title: Pouget, Sarmiento and Malbec
history.text: Following Domingo Faustino Sarmiento's plan, the project for Mendoza's Quinta Normal de Agricultura is presented to the provincial legislature; its director, the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, brings French vine varieties including Malbec. The date is now celebrated as Malbec World Day.

history.title: The railway reaches Mendoza
history.text: The Buenos Aires to Mendoza railway opens, championed by governor Tiburcio Benegas, owner of El Trapiche. Italian and Spanish immigrants pour into Cuyo, and wine for the booming capital becomes Mendoza's industry.

history.title: Nicola Catena plants Malbec
history.text: Italian immigrant Nicola Catena plants his first Malbec vineyard in Rivadavia, Eastern Mendoza, founding the family firm that his grandson Nicolás would turn into Argentina's best-known fine-wine house.

history.title: Wine in Patagonia
history.text: Humberto Canale plants vines in the Alto Valle of Río Negro, beginning commercial Patagonian viticulture.

history.title: INV and Chandon
history.text: Law 14.878 creates the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura to regulate the industry; the same year Moët & Chandon chooses Argentina for its first winery outside France.

history.title: Boom and bust
history.text: Per-capita consumption peaks near 90 litres a year in the 1970s; then consumption falls, inflation soars and vast areas of old vines, Malbec included, are uprooted or grafted to high-yielding pink grapes.

history.title: Modernisation and altitude
history.text: Economic stabilisation brings foreign investment and flying winemakers. Nicolás Catena plants the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary (1992); Michel Rolland and partners begin Clos de los Siete in Vista Flores (1998); the Uco Valley boom starts.

history.title: Law 25.163: IP, IG and DOC
history.text: The national law creates Argentina's appellation system of Indicación de Procedencia, Indicación Geográfica and Denominación de Origen Controlada, regulated by Decree 57/2004; the large IG list follows in 2002.

history.title: Wine becomes the national drink; Paraje Altamira
history.text: Law 26.870 declares wine Argentina's national drink. The same year INV recognises Paraje Altamira, the first Uco district IG drawn after soil-pit studies, opening the era of geology-based IGs.

history.title: Zuccardi Valle de Uco
history.text: The Zuccardi family opens its stone winery at Paraje Altamira, built from the alluvial rocks of its own vineyards; it is later named the World's Best Vineyard three years running.

history.title: New IGs from Patagonia to Jujuy
history.text: INV recognises El Hoyo (Chubut), Tamberías, Hilario and Sorocayense (Calingasta), Tandil (Buenos Aires), Valle de Pucará (Salta), Alto Agrelo (Luján de Cuyo) and Valles Templados (Jujuy).

history.title: A short harvest
history.text: INV reports an 18.6 million quintal grape harvest, among the lowest on record, and 9.7 million hl of wine; Argentina also sets the rules for protecting Mercosur partners' wine GIs under the 2019 Bento Gonçalves agreement.

country.classification:
Argentina's appellation law is Law 25.163 of 1999, regulated by Decree 57/2004 and administered by the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura (INV). It creates three tiers. An *Indicación de Procedencia* (IP) is for table and regional wines with at least 80% of grapes from the named area. An *Indicación Geográfica* (IG) is for quality wines from a region, locality or area no larger than a province (or an established interprovincial zone) whose character is mainly due to its origin; grapes must be grown and the wine made in the area. A *Denominación de Origen Controlada* (DOC) requires that quality be due 'exclusively or essentially' to the place, natural and human factors combined, with a regulatory council and production rules.

In practice, the IG is what matters. INV's register held 110 IGs and 2 DOCs in 2023, and at least eight more IGs have been added since (El Hoyo, Tamberías, Hilario, Sorocayense, Tandil, Valle de Pucará, Alto Agrelo, Valles Templados). They nest loosely: interprovincial regions (Cuyo, Patagonia, Valles Calchaquíes, Valles del Famatina), provinces (Mendoza, San Juan, Salta), departments (Luján de Cuyo, Tupungato, Cafayate) and districts or *parajes* (Agrelo, Los Chacayes, Paraje Altamira, San Pablo). Many department IGs were registered in bulk in 2002, while the district IGs of the 2010s and 2020s were drawn on soil, geology and climate studies. Since INV Resolution 56/2024, wineries in an area with a department or provincial IG can use it automatically. Gualtallary, Argentina's most famous district, has long been labelled under a provisional 'mención precaria' while its boundaries are argued over.

Only two DOCs exist, Luján de Cuyo (Malbec-focused, the only one in regular use) and San Rafael (2007). Varietal labels require 85% of the named grape. Under INV rules, 'Reserva' and 'Gran Reserva' are tied to minimum ageing periods, but they do not imply a particular origin.
country.climate_soils:
The climate is continental desert modified by altitude. Mendoza averages around 200 mm of rain a year, most of it falling in summer thunderstorms that bring hail (*la piedra*), the industry's great hazard, which is why many vineyards sit under anti-hail nets. The Zonda, a hot, dry foehn wind off the Andes, can damage flowering in spring. Day-night temperature swings of 15 to 20°C are normal, and low humidity keeps fungal disease rare, so organic farming is easy. In the north, the Calchaquí valleys add extreme altitude and ultraviolet light; in Patagonia, latitude, constant wind and long summer days take over; and on the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires, the ocean.

Soils are young and alluvial: fans of stones, gravel, sand and silt washed out of the Andes by rivers and flash floods. Near the mountains the fans are coarse, with rounded boulders often coated in white calcium carbonate (caliche), which drains fast and stresses the vine; further from the mountains the material becomes deep sand and silt, fertile and easy to irrigate. That gradient, more than latitude, explains why Uco Valley and Luján de Cuyo Malbec taste so different from Eastern Mendoza's. Organic matter is very low everywhere, and the sandy soils are one reason phylloxera never became the catastrophe it was elsewhere.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.note: Argentina's signature: 47,064 ha in 2024 (INV), 23.5% of all vines and the most planted variety, from Salta to Patagonia. Brought from France via Pouget's Quinta Normal in 1853; it thrives in the high Andean light, giving dark, violet-scented, plush wines.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.note: Argentina's second red, genetically the Douce Noir of Savoie (Charbono in California), not the Bonarda of Piedmont. Juicy and soft; old-vine Bonarda from Eastern Mendoza and San Rafael is a cult value red.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Planted throughout Cuyo and Salta; firmer and more herbal at altitude, often blended with Malbec.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: The rising star of Uco and Gualtallary since the 2010s, with fresh herbal lift on calcareous soils.

grapes.name: Criolla Grande and Cereza
grapes.note: Pink-skinned Criolla grapes of colonial descent, still major in the East and San Juan for bulk wine, juice and concentrate.

grapes.name: Criolla Chica
grapes.note: Listán Prieto, the original colonial grape (Chile's País, California's Mission), revived by small producers in Salta, Calingasta and Mendoza for light, earthy reds.

grapes.name: Torrontés Riojano
grapes.note: Argentina's own aromatic white, a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica; at its best in Cafayate and the Famatina valley. Torrontés Sanjuanino and Mendocino are separate, lesser varieties.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: Especially associated with San Juan's warm Tulum and Pedernal valleys.

grapes.name: Pedro Giménez
grapes.note: A widely planted white for everyday wine and concentrate, distinct from Spain's Pedro Ximénez.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: From Gualtallary and San Pablo come some of South America's most precise Chardonnays; also the backbone of Mendoza sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Old vines in Río Negro (Chacra, Noemía's neighbours) and high Uco sites; the main red for traditional-method sparkling.

grapes.name: Semillon
grapes.note: Old-vine Semillon in Uco (La Consulta) and Río Negro is a revived treasure.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: Grown in Salta's Calchaquí valleys, where altitude softens its tannins.

regions.name: Mendoza
regions.tagline: Argentina's wine heartland: 142,800 ha of irrigated vines between the Andes and the desert.
regions.summary: Mendoza holds more than 70% of Argentina's vineyards and grapes. Its five broad zones are the historic Primera Zona of Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, the high Uco Valley, the warm eastern plain, the southern oasis of San Rafael and General Alvear, and the northern desert of Lavalle.
regions.history: Founded in 1561, Mendoza drank and sold wine from the colonial era, but it became the national wine province after the 1853 Quinta Normal, the 1885 railway and mass Italian and Spanish immigration. The 1990s turned it into an international fine-wine region.
regions.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Andes, stony near the mountains and sandy to the east; 500 to 1,600 m; about 200 mm of mostly summer rain; hail, frost and the Zonda wind are the main hazards.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Criolla Grande, Cereza, Chardonnay, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez.
regions.styles: Red above all, plus traditional-method sparkling, Chardonnay and bulk wine.
regions.classification: Provincial IG > department IGs > district IGs; DOCs Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael.

regions.name: Luján de Cuyo and Maipú
regions.tagline: The Primera Zona: old-vine Malbec on the terraces of the Mendoza river.
regions.summary: Just south of Mendoza city, Luján de Cuyo and Maipú form the traditional first zone of Argentine fine wine, at 750 to 1,100 m along the Mendoza river. Luján holds the country's first DOC and more Malbec than any other department.
regions.history: Italian, Spanish and French families planted here from the late 19th century; Trapiche, López, Lagarde, Norton, Escorihuela and Weinert are among its historic houses, and Catena built its pyramid in Agrelo in the late 1990s.
regions.terroir: Stony alluvial soils near the river (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Lunlunta, Drummond), deeper clay-loam to the south (Agrelo, Perdriel, Ugarteche).
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot.
regions.styles: Classic, ripe, velvety Malbec; Cabernet blends; sparkling wine.
regions.classification: DOC Luján de Cuyo; IGs Luján de Cuyo, Agrelo, Alto Agrelo, Las Compuertas, Vistalba, Maipú, Lunlunta, Barrancas, Russel, El Paraíso.

regions.name: Valle de Uco
regions.tagline: High, cool and stony: the valley that redefined Argentine Malbec.
regions.summary: The Uco Valley spans Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos at 900 to 1,600 m, about 100 km south-west of Mendoza city. It is the most used IG in Argentina and the home of the country's most detailed terroir mapping.
regions.history: Fruit-growing country until the 1990s, when Catena's Adrianna vineyard (1992), Clos de los Siete (1998), Salentein and others proved its potential. District IGs followed from 2012, and Zuccardi's 2016 winery at Paraje Altamira became a symbol.
regions.terroir: Alluvial fans of stones, sand and calcium carbonate; cold nights, frost and hail; strong UV light.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Fresh, floral, chalky Malbec; precise Chardonnay; sparkling base.
regions.classification: Interdepartmental IG Valle de Uco > departments Tupungato, Tunuyán, San Carlos > districts Gualtallary (provisional), El Peral, Los Chacayes, Vista Flores, San Pablo, Paraje Altamira, Pampa El Cepillo, Cordón del Cepillo, La Consulta.

regions.name: East Mendoza
regions.tagline: The volume engine: hot plains, old Bonarda and the Catena family's first vineyard.
regions.summary: Eastern Mendoza (San Martín, Junín, Rivadavia, Santa Rosa, La Paz) holds the largest vineyard area in Argentina on flat, hot plains at 600 to 750 m. It produces most of the country's everyday wine, juice and concentrate, and old-vine Bonarda and Malbec of real character.
regions.history: Settled by Italian and Spanish immigrants after the railway; Nicola Catena planted his first Malbec at Rivadavia in 1902.
regions.terroir: Deep sandy and silty alluvium; warmer and lower than western Mendoza.
regions.grapes: Bonarda, Malbec, Criolla Grande, Cereza, Pedro Giménez, Syrah.
regions.classification: Department IGs plus district IGs Distrito Medrano and Reducción.

regions.name: San Rafael and General Alvear
regions.tagline: Mendoza's southern oasis, home of Argentina's second DOC.
regions.summary: The southern oasis of the Diamante and Atuel rivers at 450 to 800 m, about 230 km from Mendoza city. San Rafael has been a DOC since 2007 and is known for fresh, fairly priced reds and sparkling wines.
regions.history: French, Italian and Spanish immigrants built the oasis from the late 19th century; Valentín Bianchi's family winery dates from 1928.
regions.terroir: Alluvial soils, cooler than eastern Mendoza thanks to latitude.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chenin Blanc, Syrah.
regions.classification: DOC San Rafael; IGs San Rafael and General Alvear.

regions.name: San Juan
regions.tagline: Desert Syrah in the Tulum oasis and high-mountain wine in Calingasta and Pedernal.
regions.summary: Argentina's second wine province, about 39,700 ha, mostly in the hot Tulum valley around the capital, plus the high valleys of Pedernal, Zonda and Calingasta.
regions.history: Vines arrived in the 1560s; the province became a grape, raisin and wine powerhouse after the railway; Syrah took on a provincial identity from the 1990s; three Calingasta IGs were added in 2024.
regions.terroir: Desert climate with under 100 mm of rain; alluvial soils on the Tulum floor; stony, calcareous soils at 1,300 to 1,700 m in Pedernal and Calingasta.
regions.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Bonarda, Cereza, Criolla, Pedro Giménez, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés Sanjuanino.
regions.styles: Generous Syrah and Malbec; fresh mountain reds; raisins and juice.

regions.name: La Rioja
regions.tagline: Torrontés Riojano's homeland in the Famatina valleys.
regions.summary: La Rioja's wine is concentrated in the Famatina valleys around Chilecito at 1,000 to 1,700 m, the birthplace of Torrontés Riojano. The province's IG carries 'Argentina' in its name to distinguish it from Spain's Rioja.
regions.history: Colonial vineyards for wine and aguardiente; 20th-century cooperatives, especially La Riojana in Chilecito.
regions.terroir: Arid valleys between the Famatina and Velasco ranges; alluvial soils; hot days, cool nights.
regions.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon.

regions.summary: Catamarca's vineyards lie in the Fiambalá and Tinogasta valleys, around Belén, Pomán and in Santa María at the southern end of the Calchaquí valleys.
regions.history: Colonial vineyards and adobe wineries; a revival of home-made *vino patero* and modern altitude projects.
regions.terroir: Desert valleys at 1,200 to 2,000 m; sandy and stony soils.
regions.classification: Provincial IG > department IGs Tinogasta, Belén, Pomán, Santa María.

regions.name: Salta
regions.tagline: The Calchaquí valleys: Torrontés at Cafayate and Malbec above 3,000 m.
regions.summary: Salta's vineyards sit almost entirely in the Calchaquí valleys from Cafayate (1,700 m) to Cachi and Payogasta (over 3,000 m). Malbec covers 46% of the vineyard; Torrontés from Cafayate is the regional signature.
regions.history: Jesuits and Spanish settlers planted Criolla; Colomé was founded in 1831 and planted French Malbec and Cabernet in the 1850s; Swiss Donald Hess bought it in 2001 and planted the 3,111 m Altura Máxima vineyard.
regions.terroir: Sandy and gravelly alluvium, granite slopes; extreme UV, cold nights, under 200 mm of rain.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica.
regions.styles: Floral Torrontés; deep, tannic altitude reds.
regions.classification: Provincial IG Salta; interprovincial Valles Calchaquíes; Valle de Cafayate, Molinos, Cachi, San Carlos, Valle de Pucará.

regions.history: A modern project scene from the 2000s around Maimará, Tilcara and Huacalera.
regions.terroir: Stony alluvial terraces, extreme altitude and light.
regions.styles: Small volumes of intense mountain reds.

regions.name: Patagonia
regions.tagline: Wind, cold nights and old vines along the Río Negro.
regions.summary: Patagonian wine is centred on the Alto Valle of the Río Negro and the San Patricio del Chañar plateau in Neuquén, with outposts in La Pampa and Chubut down to 45°S.
regions.history: Humberto Canale planted in 1909; old Malbec, Merlot and Pinot Noir vineyards of the 1930s to 1950s were rediscovered by Noemía (2001) and Chacra (2004); Neuquén's desert projects date from the late 1990s.
regions.terroir: Irrigated river valleys at 250 to 400 m; alluvial soils; constant wind, cool nights, long summer days.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Fresh, perfumed reds; Pinot Noir; crisp whites; sparkling wine in Chubut.
regions.classification: Interprovincial IG Patagonia; provincial IGs Neuquén and Río Negro; Alto Valle de Río Negro; department IGs; Chubut IGs Trevelin, El Hoyo, Sarmiento.

regions.name: Córdoba
regions.summary: Córdoba's small wine area sits around Colonia Caroya and Jesús María, the Traslasierra valley and Cruz del Eje.
regions.history: Jesuit estancias made wine from the 17th century; Friulian immigrants founded Colonia Caroya in 1878.
regions.terroir: Sierras and piedmont plains with summer rain.
regions.grapes: Isabella (for Frambua), Malbec and other vinifera.
regions.styles: Traditional Frambua and small-scale vinifera wines.
regions.classification: Provincial IG Córdoba Argentina; IGs Colón, Colonia Caroya, Cruz del Eje, San Javier.

sources.title: INV, Indicaciones Geográficas y Denominaciones de Origen reconocidas y protegidas de la República Argentina (register list)

regions.name: Buenos Aires
regions.tagline: Atlantic and Pampas hill vineyards on the new frontier.
regions.summary: Buenos Aires province has a young wine scene in the Ventania and Tandilia hills and at Chapadmalal on the Atlantic coast, plus Médanos in the south-west.
regions.history: Mostly 21st-century projects; Trapiche's coastal vineyard at Chapadmalal and IGs from 2011 (Villa Ventana) to 2024 (Tandil).
regions.terroir: Cool, humid maritime and Pampas climates; loess and stony hill soils.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Malbec.
regions.styles: Saline whites, light reds, sparkling wine.
regions.classification: IGs Chapadmalal, Villa Ventana, Balcarce, Tandil.

INV, Indicaciones Geográficas y Denominaciones de Origen reconocidas y protegidas de la República Argentina (register list)

ar-25-de-mayo.name: 25 de Mayo
ar-25-de-mayo.summary: Veinticinco de Mayo is one of San Juan's largest vineyard departments, south-east of the capital in the Tulum valley, about 7,700 ha of vines in 2024 (INV), much of it for bulk wine and juice.

ar-9-de-julio.name: 9 de Julio
ar-9-de-julio.summary: Nueve de Julio is a Tulum-valley department east of San Juan city with about 2,800 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly traditional varieties.

ar-agrelo.name: Agrelo
ar-agrelo.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay
ar-agrelo.nerd_note: The pyramid at Catena Zapata, designed by Pablo Sánchez Elía and built in the late 1990s, was inspired by Mayan temples.
ar-agrelo.summary: Agrelo, a district in southern Luján de Cuyo at 950 to 1,100 m, is one of the most planted fine-wine zones in Argentina and the home of Catena Zapata's pyramid winery and its La Pirámide vineyard (planted 1983). Deeper clay-loam soils with stones below give dense, dark, plush Malbec and good Cabernet Sauvignon; frost and hail are risks on the open plain. Agrelo was the eighth most used IG for exports in 2022 (INV).

ar-albardon.name: Albardón
ar-albardon.summary: Albardón, just north of San Juan city along the river, has about 1,400 ha of vines (INV 2024), many for table grapes and raisins.

ar-alto-agrelo.name: Alto Agrelo
ar-alto-agrelo.summary: Alto Agrelo became Argentina's newest Luján de Cuyo IG in July 2025, at the request of Grupo Avinea, whose 232-ha organic estate there is the source of Argento's estate Malbecs. It covers the higher, western part of Agrelo towards the Andean foothills, where stonier soils and cooler nights give fresher Malbec than the classic Agrelo plain. It joins Luján de Cuyo, Agrelo, Las Compuertas and Vistalba as the fifth IG within the department.

ar-alto-valle-de-rio-negro.name: Alto valle de Río Negro
ar-alto-valle-de-rio-negro.summary: The Alto Valle is the irrigated upper valley of the Río Negro from the Neuquén-Limay confluence east past General Roca, an apple-and-pear oasis at about 250 to 300 m. Humberto Canale planted vines here in 1909, and old Malbec, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Semillon from mid-20th-century plantings now attract fine-wine producers. Cool nights, constant wind and long summer days give fresh, perfumed wines.

ar-anelo.name: Añelo
ar-anelo.summary: Añelo department in Neuquén contains San Patricio del Chañar, where from the late 1990s irrigation turned desert plateau into vineyards for Bodega del Fin del Mundo, Familia Schroeder and NQN; it holds 89% of Neuquén's Malbec (INV 2024).

ar-angaco.name: Angaco
ar-angaco.summary: Angaco, north-east of San Juan city, has about 2,100 ha of vines (INV 2024) in the Tulum oasis.

ar-arauco.name: Arauco
ar-arauco.summary: Arauco, around Aimogasta in northern La Rioja, is olive country first; its IG covers small vineyards of traditional varieties.

ar-avellaneda.name: Avellaneda
ar-avellaneda.summary: Avellaneda department, in the middle Río Negro valley around Choele Choel, grows pears, apples and a little wine; about 58 ha of Malbec (INV 2024).

ar-balcarce.name: Balcarce
ar-balcarce.summary: Balcarce, in the Tandilia hills of south-eastern Buenos Aires province, was recognised in 2022 at the request of the area's one significant winery. It is cool, humid Pampas country suited to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base.

ar-barrancas.name: Barrancas
ar-barrancas.summary: Barrancas, in eastern Maipú on the banks of the Mendoza river, is a warm district of old vineyards known for ripe Malbec, Syrah and Bonarda. It was among the first Maipú districts registered as an IG, and among the most exported of small IGs in 2022.

ar-barreal.name: Barreal
ar-barreal.summary: Barreal, at about 1,650 m at the southern end of the Calingasta valley under the Mercedario peak, is one of the highest IGs in Cuyo. Cara Sur makes light, mountain Criolla and Bonarda here from old vines trained on parral.

ar-belen.name: Belén
ar-belen.summary: Belén, in central-western Catamarca, grows grapes in small Andean oases such as Hualfín and Londres at 1,200 to 1,800 m.

ar-cachi.name: Cachi
ar-cachi.summary: Cachi, in the upper Calchaquí valley at about 2,300 to 3,000 m under the Nevado de Cachi, has about 117 ha of vines (INV 2024), 73% Malbec. Vineyards at Cachi Adentro and Payogasta are among the highest in the world.

ar-cafayate.name: Valle de Cafayate
ar-cafayate.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; only 'Valle de Cafayate' allowed since 2005)
ar-cafayate.summary: Cafayate is the wine town of the Calchaquí valleys, at about 1,700 to 2,000 m, with roughly 2,765 ha of vines (INV 2024), three-quarters of Salta's total. Its sandy, wind-scoured terraces under the red sandstone of the Quebrada de las Conchas give Argentina's best Torrontés, aromatic yet dry, and dense, sun-built Malbec, Cabernet and Tannat. Wineries such as El Esteco, Etchart, El Porvenir and Michel Rolland's Yacochuya line the town. Because 'Cafayate' is a registered trademark, INV ruled in 2005 that only the form 'Valle de Cafayate' may be used on labels.

ar-calingasta.name: Calingasta
ar-calingasta.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Valle de Calingasta 2013)
ar-calingasta.summary: Calingasta is San Juan's spectacular Andean valley, a north-south trough at 1,350 to 1,700 m between the main cordillera and the pre-cordillera, reached by a mountain road from San Juan. Only about 250 ha of vines (INV 2024), two-thirds of them Malbec, grow around Calingasta, Tamberías and Barreal on stony soils with huge day-night swings, giving deep-coloured, fresh reds. Since 2024 the valley has three more sub-IGs, Tamberías, Hilario and Sorocayense.

ar-canota.name: Canota
ar-canota.nerd_note: The site sits near the Canota monument, which marks where San Martín's Army of the Andes split its columns in 1817.
ar-canota.summary: Canota (Valle de Canota) is a small piedmont IG in Las Heras, north-west of Mendoza city on the old road to Villavicencio, recognised in 2020. Vineyards here at over 1,000 m sit on alluvial fans of the pre-cordillera, a cooler, stonier frontier for Malbec.

ar-castro-barros.name: Castro Barros
ar-castro-barros.summary: Castro Barros, in the valleys north of La Rioja city, has about 70 ha of Malbec among small traditional vineyards (INV 2024).

ar-catamarca.name: Catamarca
ar-catamarca.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Syrah, Criolla, Cabernet Sauvignon
ar-catamarca.summary: Catamarca's provincial IG covers about 2,700 ha of vines (INV 2024) in high Andean valleys: Fiambalá and Tinogasta in the west, Belén and Santa María in the north (where the Calchaquí valleys begin), and Pomán. Old Criolla and Torrontés vines, home-made *vino patero* and new altitude Malbec and Syrah share the landscape.

ar-caucete.name: Caucete
ar-caucete.summary: Caucete, east of the San Juan river, is one of the province's big vineyard departments (about 6,700 ha in 2024, INV) and second only to Sarmiento for Malbec in San Juan.

ar-chapadmalal.name: Chapadmalal
ar-chapadmalal.summary: Chapadmalal, on the Atlantic coast south of Mar del Plata, is Argentina's maritime wine experiment: Trapiche planted vineyards here around 2010 a few kilometres from the sea, and the IG followed in 2014. Cool, humid, windy conditions on loess soils give Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with real salinity, sold as Costa & Pampa.

ar-chilecito.name: Chilecito
ar-chilecito.summary: Chilecito is La Rioja's wine capital and the core of the Famatina valleys, with about 580 ha of Malbec and much more Torrontés Riojano; La Riojana cooperative is based here, and the town still has the cableway built in 1904 to carry ore from the Famatina mines.

ar-chimbas.name: Chimbas
ar-chimbas.summary: Chimbas, on the northern edge of San Juan city, is a small, largely urban wine department with about 700 ha of vines (INV 2024).

ar-colon.name: Colón
ar-colon.summary: Colón department, north of Córdoba city, contains Colonia Caroya and Jesús María, the historic core of Córdoba wine.

ar-colonia-caroya.name: Colonia Caroya
ar-colonia-caroya.nerd_note: The nearby Estancia Jesuítica de Caroya, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, made wine for the Jesuit college of Córdoba from the 17th century.
ar-colonia-caroya.summary: Colonia Caroya was settled in 1878 by immigrants from Friuli, who planted vines on land of the former Jesuit estancia of Caroya. They still make Frambua, a sweetish red from the American hybrid Isabella, alongside vinifera wines, and celebrate a harvest festival each year.

ar-confluencia.name: Confluencia
ar-confluencia.summary: Confluencia, the department around Neuquén city where the Neuquén and Limay rivers meet, has small vineyards near Plottier and Centenario.

ar-cordoba-argentina.name: Córdoba Argentina
ar-cordoba-argentina.summary: Córdoba's provincial IG (with 'Argentina' added to separate it from Spain's Córdoba) covers about 240 ha of vines (INV 2024). The province's wine history is Jesuit and Italian: the Jesuit estancias of the 17th and 18th centuries made wine, and Friulian immigrants at Colonia Caroya still make Frambua from American hybrid grapes.

ar-cordon-el-cepillo.name: Cordón el Cepillo
ar-cordon-el-cepillo.summary: Cordón del Cepillo, recognised in 2022, is a higher piedmont zone in San Carlos along the Cepillo range, west of Pampa El Cepillo. It is one of the newest Uco frontiers, with very stony soils and cool conditions.

ar-cruz-del-eje.name: Cruz del Eje
ar-cruz-del-eje.summary: Cruz del Eje, in north-western Córdoba, is a warm valley with a small grape-growing tradition.

ar-cuyo.name: Cuyo
ar-cuyo.grapes: Malbec, Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez
ar-cuyo.summary: Cuyo is the interprovincial IG covering Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis, the historic western heartland that makes the vast majority of Argentine wine. The name comes from the Huarpe word for 'sandy land' or 'desert country', and the region is exactly that: an irrigated oasis economy at the foot of the Andes. As an IG it is rarely seen on serious labels, which prefer a province or a district.

ar-distrito-medrano.name: Distrito Medrano
ar-distrito-medrano.summary: Medrano, straddling Rivadavia and Junín in Eastern Mendoza, was recognised as an IG in 2014. Its stony soils near the Tunuyán river give more structured Malbec and Bonarda than the typical eastern plain.

ar-el-hoyo.name: El Hoyo
ar-el-hoyo.summary: El Hoyo, a pre-Andean valley in the far north of Chubut near El Bolsón at only about 300 m, became an IG in September 2023 at the request of Patagonian Wines, the estate founded by Bernardo Weinert. Its roughly 28 ha grow Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and Gewürztraminer at latitude 42°S.

ar-el-paraiso.name: El Paraíso
ar-el-paraiso.summary: El Paraíso is a small IG in Maipú's Fray Luis Beltrán area, along the Mendoza river, recognised in 2007 for its traditional red-wine vineyards.

ar-el-peral.name: El Peral
ar-el-peral.summary: El Peral is a district of Tupungato at about 1,100 to 1,300 m, recognised as an IG at the request of Bodegas Chandon. Chandon grows sparkling-base Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here; cool nights and stony soils also give fresh Malbec.

ar-famatina.name: Famatina
ar-famatina.summary: Famatina department, north of Chilecito under the snow-capped Famatina range, grows Torrontés and Malbec at 1,400 to 1,700 m; it contains the Valle de Chañarmuyo IG.

ar-felipe-varela.name: Felipe Varela
ar-felipe-varela.summary: Coronel Felipe Varela department, around Villa Unión in western La Rioja, grows grapes in an arid basin near the Talampaya canyon.

ar-general-alvear.name: General Alvear
ar-general-alvear.summary: General Alvear, east of San Rafael on the Atuel river, is Mendoza's southernmost wine department, with about 3,100 ha (INV 2024) of mostly traditional varieties and everyday wine.

ar-general-conesa.name: General Conesa
ar-general-conesa.summary: General Conesa, on the lower Río Negro, is a small irrigated area with a few vineyards.

ar-general-lamadrid.name: General Lamadrid
ar-general-lamadrid.summary: General Lamadrid is a remote high department in western La Rioja with a few hectares of vines.

ar-general-roca.name: General Roca
ar-general-roca.summary: General Roca department is the core of Río Negro wine, along the Alto Valle with about 215 ha of Malbec (INV 2024); it includes Mainqué, home of Noemía and Chacra.

ar-godoy-cruz.name: Godoy Cruz
ar-godoy-cruz.summary: Godoy Cruz, now part of Greater Mendoza, was a 19th-century wine town. It keeps historic wineries such as Escorihuela Gascón (founded 1884) and Bodega Arizu, though the IG's vineyards have almost all given way to the city.

ar-gualtallary.name: Gualtallary
ar-gualtallary.created: Provisional ('mención precaria'), INV; definitive status unconfirmed
ar-gualtallary.grapes: Malbec, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir
ar-gualtallary.nerd_note: In 2022 wines labelled Gualtallary exported 438,207 litres at an average US$7.1 per litre, ninth among Argentine IGs (INV).
ar-gualtallary.summary:
Gualtallary, a district of Tupungato rising from about 1,200 to 1,600 m, is the closest thing Argentina has to a grand cru. Nicolás Catena's Adrianna vineyard, planted in 1992 at about 1,450 m when everyone said the site was too cold, gave the world-famous Adrianna Malbecs and White Bones and White Stones Chardonnays. Soils are shallow alluvial gravels and sand over limestone (calcium carbonate) crusts, sometimes with fossil-bearing caliche; the light is intense and the nights cold.

Gualtallary wines are electric: violet-scented, chalk-textured Malbec, taut Chardonnay, and Cabernet Franc with herbal lift. Zuccardi, El Enemigo, SuperUco and Huentala all farm here. Its IG application ran into disputes over the boundary; INV's 2023 statistics list it as a 'mención precaria' (a provisional authorisation to label) and I found no confirmation of definitive registration as of October 2026.

ar-guaymallen.name: Guaymallén
ar-guaymallen.summary: Guaymallén, on the eastern side of Mendoza city, is a historic wine department now largely urban; under 500 ha of vines remain (INV 2024), mostly Malbec and Criolla.

ar-hilario.name: Hilario
ar-hilario.summary: Hilario is a small locality in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG together with Tamberías and Sorocayense in early 2024 to protect the names of the valley's distinct high-altitude terroirs.

ar-iglesia.name: Iglesia
ar-iglesia.summary: Iglesia is a high Andean department in north-western San Juan, around 1,600 to 1,900 m, with only a few hectares of vines (INV 2024) in an oasis landscape of poplars and adobe villages.

ar-jachal.name: Jáchal
ar-jachal.summary: Jáchal, in northern San Juan, is a historic agricultural oasis at about 1,150 m known for onions and wine; vineyards are now small.

ar-jujuy.name: Jujuy
ar-jujuy.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Merlot, Criolla
ar-jujuy.summary: Jujuy, Argentina's northernmost wine province, has only about 70 ha of vines (INV 2024) but some of the most spectacular: terraces in the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO World Heritage valley, at 2,300 to over 3,000 m. Since 2025 a second IG, Valles Templados, covers the lower, temperate valleys around San Salvador and Perico.

ar-junin.name: Junín
ar-junin.summary: Junín, in Eastern Mendoza, has about 10,800 ha of vines (INV 2024) and a reputation for generous Bonarda and Malbec from warm, sandy soils.

ar-la-consulta.name: La Consulta
ar-la-consulta.summary: La Consulta, a district of San Carlos at about 950 to 1,100 m, is old Malbec country: dozens of growers farm vineyards planted in the mid-20th century on deep alluvial soils. It was recognised in 2014 at the request of Leoncio Arizu, and many of the region's best old-vine Malbecs are sourced here.

ar-la-paz.name: La Paz
ar-la-paz.summary: La Paz is Mendoza's easternmost wine department, hot and dry on the border with San Luis, with only about 135 ha of vines (INV 2024).

ar-la-rioja-argentina.name: La Rioja Argentina
ar-la-rioja-argentina.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
ar-la-rioja-argentina.nerd_note: Torrontés Riojano is a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Listán Prieto (Criolla Chica), born in the New World.
ar-la-rioja-argentina.summary: La Rioja's provincial IG carries 'Argentina' in its name to avoid any confusion with Spain's Rioja. The province has about 7,000 ha of vines (INV 2024), concentrated in the Famatina valley around Chilecito, and is the homeland of Torrontés Riojano, the most aromatic and widely planted of Argentina's three Torrontés grapes. Large cooperatives such as La Riojana dominate production.

ar-las-compuertas.name: Las Compuertas
ar-las-compuertas.nerd_note: 'Las Compuertas' means 'the floodgates', after the colonial sluices that diverted the Mendoza river into irrigation canals.
ar-las-compuertas.summary: Las Compuertas, at about 1,050 m on the north side of Luján de Cuyo by the Mendoza river, holds some of Argentina's oldest Malbec vineyards, many planted in the early 20th century and still own-rooted. Poor, stony alluvial soils and the cooling effect of the river's canyon give fragrant, fine-grained Malbec. Cheval des Andes and many old-vine cuvées source here.

ar-las-heras.name: Las Heras
ar-las-heras.summary: Las Heras stretches from Mendoza city north-west into the high Andes along the road to Chile. Its vineyards (about 1,300 ha in 2024) lie near the city; the separate Canota IG covers a higher piedmont site.

ar-lavalle.name: Lavalle
ar-lavalle.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Desierto de Lavalle 2009)
ar-lavalle.summary: Lavalle, north of Mendoza city, is the province's driest and lowest wine department (around 600 m), with about 12,300 ha of vines (INV 2024) for bulk wine, juice and grape concentrate. The synonym 'Desierto de Lavalle' was added in 2009 for wines from its sandy, desert vineyards.

ar-los-chacayes.name: Los Chacayes
ar-los-chacayes.summary: Los Chacayes is an alluvial fan at 1,100 to 1,600 m in western Tunuyán, recognised as an IG in 2017. Its soils are among the stoniest in Uco, with big river boulders and little fine material, and the vines struggle: Malbec here is dark, tannic and mountain-fresh. François Lurton's Bodega Piedra Negra and Corazón del Sol are among the estates here.

ar-lujan-de-cuyo.name: Luján de Cuyo
ar-lujan-de-cuyo.created: DOC 1989/1993 (sources differ); registered by INV Res. C.15/2005
ar-lujan-de-cuyo.grapes: Malbec (8,920 ha of the department's 15,210 ha in 2024), Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot
ar-lujan-de-cuyo.terroir: Alluvial terraces of the Mendoza river, stony near the river in the north, deeper clay-loam over gravel to the south; 850 to 1,100 m; about 200 mm of rain, wide day-night swings.
ar-lujan-de-cuyo.nerd_note: Luján de Cuyo holds about 22% of all Malbec in Mendoza, more than any other department (INV 2025 Malbec report).
ar-lujan-de-cuyo.summary:
Luján de Cuyo is Argentina's first denomination of origin and the historic home of fine Malbec. The department lies just south of Mendoza city on the first terrace of the Mendoza river at 850 to 1,100 m, and from the late 19th century its districts (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Chacras de Coria, Mayor Drummond, Perdriel, Agrelo, Ugarteche) were planted by Italian, Spanish and French families. Many vineyards are 60 to over 100 years old and own-rooted.

The DOC was pushed through by local producers in the late 1980s and early 1990s to defend Malbec's reputation; INV registered it under the 1999 national law in 2005. It is the only Argentine DOC in regular use: INV reported 382,866 litres exported and 511,537 litres sold domestically under the DOC in 2022. Its terroir divides north to south. The northern districts near the river (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Chacras, Drummond) have stony alluvial soils and give perfumed, elegant Malbec. The southern districts of Perdriel, Agrelo and Ugarteche have deeper clay-loam and give broader, darker wines. Agrelo, Las Compuertas, Vistalba and Alto Agrelo also have their own IGs.

Luján Malbec is the classic Argentine style: plum, violet and mocha, ripe and velvety, built for ageing in the best old-vine cuvées.

ar-lujan-de-cuyo-2.name: Luján de Cuyo (IG)
ar-lujan-de-cuyo-2.summary: Alongside the DOC, the department of Luján de Cuyo is also registered as a plain IG with identical limits. The IG lets producers name the department without meeting the DOC's extra rules, and most Luján wines on export shelves use it this way.

ar-lunlunta.name: Lunlunta
ar-lunlunta.summary: Lunlunta is a riverside district of Maipú, on high terraces above the Mendoza river at about 900 m. Old Malbec here, including Catena's Angélica vineyard planted in the 1920s, grows on stony alluvium and gives deep but fresh wines.

ar-maipu.name: Maipú
ar-maipu.summary: Maipú, east of Luján de Cuyo along the Mendoza river at 750 to 1,000 m, is the other half of Mendoza's historic Primera Zona. It is where the 19th-century wine industry concentrated after the 1885 railway arrived: Trapiche, López, Giol's La Colina de Oro and the national wine museum are here. Its riverside districts (Lunlunta, Cruz de Piedra, Barrancas, Russell) have old vineyards on stony alluvium and give classic, ripe Malbec, Cabernet and old-vine Bonarda.

ar-mendoza.name: Mendoza
ar-mendoza.grapes: Malbec (39,856 ha in 2024), Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Syrah, Chardonnay, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez
ar-mendoza.terroir: Alluvial fans of Andean rivers: stony, calcareous gravels near the mountains, deep sandy and silty soils on the eastern plain; continental desert climate with hail ('la piedra') and the hot, dry Zonda wind as the main hazards.
ar-mendoza.nerd_note: Mendoza's first vines were planted shortly after the city's founding by Pedro del Castillo on 2 March 1561.
ar-mendoza.summary:
Mendoza is the province that is Argentine wine to most of the world: about 142,800 ha of vines in 2024 (INV), more than 70% of the national vineyard and of the 2026 grape harvest. The vineyards are irrigated oases strung along the Mendoza, Tunuyán, Diamante and Atuel rivers, fed by Andean snowmelt through a canal network that began with Huarpe and Inca irrigation and was expanded by the Spanish from the 1560s. Rain is scarce (around 200 mm), sunshine abundant, and altitude does the cooling: vineyards run from about 500 m in the east to over 1,500 m in the Uco Valley.

The province has five broad zones. The Primera Zona of Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, just south of the city, is the historic fine-wine heart. The Uco Valley, 80 to 120 km south-west at 900 to 1,600 m, is the modern star. The East (San Martín, Junín, Rivadavia, Santa Rosa, La Paz) is the volume engine. San Rafael and General Alvear in the south form their own oasis, and Lavalle in the north grows mostly for bulk wine and grape juice. As an IG, 'Mendoza' on a label means the grapes come from anywhere in the province, the usual choice for blends and good-value Malbec.

ar-molinos.name: Molinos
ar-molinos.summary: Molinos is a colonial village in the middle Calchaquí valley at about 2,000 m. Its department includes Colomé, founded in 1831 and one of Argentina's oldest working wineries, whose vineyards climb from 2,300 to 3,111 m, and the small high estate of Tacuil. Malbec covers 69% of its 133 ha (INV 2024).

ar-neuquen.name: Neuquén
ar-neuquen.summary: Neuquén's provincial IG covers about 1,500 ha (INV 2024), most of it created from scratch since the late 1990s on the desert plateau of San Patricio del Chañar, north of the city of Neuquén, where large irrigation projects turned steppe into vineyard for Bodega del Fin del Mundo, Familia Schroeder and NQN. Strong winds, cool nights and long sun make dense, fresh Malbec, Pinot Noir and Merlot.

ar-pampa-el-cepillo.name: Pampa el Cepillo
ar-pampa-el-cepillo.summary: Pampa El Cepillo, recognised in 2019, is the plain south of Paraje Altamira in San Carlos, around 1,000 to 1,100 m. It is cold, frost-prone and windswept, with stony, calcareous alluvium; Malbec and Cabernet Franc ripen slowly into firm, fresh wines. Its limits were drawn on geological and climatic criteria.

ar-paraje-altamira.name: Paraje Altamira
ar-paraje-altamira.nerd_note: In 2022 Paraje Altamira wines exported at US$20.4 per litre on average, four times the national IG average (INV).
ar-paraje-altamira.summary:
Paraje Altamira is the alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river in San Carlos, at about 1,000 to 1,150 m, and Argentina's most studied terroir. Its recognition in 2013 followed five years of work including some 200 soil pits; the first zone of 4,790 ha (1,400 ha of vineyard) was later enlarged to about 9,290 ha with 2,800 ha of vines. The legal name carries 'Paraje' because 'Altamira' was a registered trademark.

The soils are a jumble of rounded river stones coated in white calcium carbonate, over sand and silt, which drain fast and push Malbec to small berries and fine, chalky tannin. Zuccardi built its Valle de Uco winery here in 2016 out of the same stones, and its Piedra Infinita Malbec comes from the fan. Catena's Nicasia vineyard and Achával-Ferrer's Finca Altamira are among the other landmarks. Paraje Altamira wines command among the highest average export prices of any Argentine IG.

ar-patagonia.name: Patagonia
ar-patagonia.grapes: Malbec, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
ar-patagonia.summary: The Patagonia IG is an interprovincial umbrella for Neuquén, Río Negro, La Pampa, Chubut and the rest of southern Argentina. It is one of the most used IGs on export labels (13% of IG wine sold in 2022, per INV), because it carries an image of cold, wind and purity. The vineyards cluster in irrigated river valleys of the Negro, Neuquén and Colorado, plus a scatter of new sites as far south as Chubut's Sarmiento at 45°S.

ar-pichimahuida.name: Pichimahuida
ar-pichimahuida.summary: Pichi Mahuida, on the Río Colorado at the north-eastern edge of Río Negro province, has a few small vineyards.

ar-pocito.name: Pocito
ar-pocito.summary: Pocito, south of San Juan city in the Tulum valley, has about 2,900 ha of vines (INV 2024) and several of the province's established wineries.

ar-poman.name: Pomán
ar-poman.summary: Pomán, at the foot of the Ambato range in Catamarca, has a few traditional vineyards around Saujil and Mutquín.

ar-pozo-de-los-algarrobos.name: Pozo de los Algarrobos
ar-pozo-de-los-algarrobos.summary: Pozo de los Algarrobos is a small IG in Caucete department, east of the San Juan river, recognised in 2015 for the vineyards of this desert locality.

ar-quebrada-de-humahuaca.name: Quebrada de Humahuaca
ar-quebrada-de-humahuaca.summary: The Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO World Heritage valley of coloured mountains in Jujuy, has a tiny modern wine scene on terraces between about 2,300 and 3,300 m around Maimará, Tilcara, Huacalera and Uquía. Fernando Dupont, Bodega Kindgard and others make Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Merlot of intense colour and freshness. It is one of the highest IGs in the world.

ar-rawson.name: Rawson
ar-rawson.summary: Rawson, a Tulum-valley department on the southern edge of San Juan city, has about 1,250 ha of vines (INV 2024).

ar-reduccion.name: Reducción
ar-reduccion.summary: La Reducción is a district of Rivadavia in Eastern Mendoza, recognised as an IG in 2020. Its name recalls a colonial *reducción*, a settlement where indigenous Huarpe people were gathered; it grows traditional reds.

ar-rio-negro.name: Río Negro
ar-rio-negro.summary: Río Negro's provincial IG covers about 1,300 ha (INV 2024), most along the irrigated Alto Valle of the Río Negro, an apple-and-pear valley where Humberto Canale planted vines in 1909. It is the source of some of Argentina's oldest Malbec, Merlot and Semillon and of Pinot Noir that convinced Italian and Danish investors (Chacra, Noemía) to settle here.

ar-rivadavia.name: Rivadavia
ar-rivadavia.summary: Rivadavia, in Eastern Mendoza along the Tunuyán river, has about 13,900 ha of vines (INV 2024). Nicola Catena planted his first Malbec here at La Libertad in 1902, and old-vine Bonarda from the East has become a cult value wine.

ar-rivadavia-2.name: Rivadavia (San Juan)
ar-rivadavia-2.summary: Rivadavia in San Juan (not to be confused with Mendoza's Rivadavia) is a mostly urban department west of the provincial capital with under 200 ha of vines (INV 2024).

ar-russel.name: Russel
ar-russel.summary: Russell (registered as 'Russel') is a district of Maipú with deep soils and long-established vineyards for Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon.

ar-salta.name: Salta
ar-salta.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica
ar-salta.summary: Salta is Argentina's altitude province: about 3,700 ha of vines (INV 2024), almost all in the Calchaquí valleys between 1,700 and 3,100 m. Malbec covers 46% of the provincial vineyard, but Salta's signature is Torrontés from Cafayate, floral and fresh, and Malbec and Tannat of deep colour and thick skins built by intense sunlight. The provincial IG appears on blends from across the valleys.

ar-san-blas-de-los-sauces.name: San Blas de los Sauces
ar-san-blas-de-los-sauces.summary: San Blas de los Sauces, in northern La Rioja, is a string of small oasis villages with traditional vineyards.

ar-san-carlos.name: San Carlos
ar-san-carlos.summary: San Carlos is the southern Uco department, about 8,800 ha of vines (INV 2024), two-thirds of them Malbec. It holds Paraje Altamira, Pampa El Cepillo, Cordón del Cepillo and La Consulta, and a long tradition of growers' cooperatives and old Malbec around La Consulta and Eugenio Bustos.

ar-san-carlos-2.name: San Carlos (Salta)
ar-san-carlos-2.summary: San Carlos department in Salta, between Cafayate and Molinos along the Calchaquí river, includes Angastaco and Animaná, with about 670 ha of vines (INV 2024). It contains the Valle de Pucará IG.

ar-san-javier.name: San Javier
ar-san-javier.summary: San Javier department, in the Traslasierra valley west of the Córdoba hills around Villa Dolores, has small vineyards at the foot of the Comechingones range.

ar-san-juan.name: San Juan
ar-san-juan.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Bonarda, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Pedro Giménez, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés
ar-san-juan.nerd_note: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, who later brought Pouget and Malbec to Mendoza's Quinta Normal, was born in San Juan in 1811.
ar-san-juan.summary: San Juan is Argentina's second wine province, about 39,700 ha of vines in 2024 (INV) and roughly a quarter of the national harvest. It is hotter, drier and lower than Mendoza: the Tulum valley around the provincial capital is a desert oasis growing grapes for wine, raisins, juice and table fruit. Its fine-wine story lives at the edges, in the high Andean valleys of Calingasta and Pedernal and the cooler Zonda valley, and in Syrah, which has had a strong San Juan identity since the 1990s.

ar-san-luis.name: San Luis
ar-san-luis.summary: San Luis is the third Cuyo province and a minor wine producer, with about 100 ha of vines (INV 2024). Its IG, recognised in 2019, covers the whole province; small projects around the capital and in the Sierras de San Luis grow Malbec and other reds at moderate altitude.

ar-san-martin.name: San Martín
ar-san-martin.summary: San Martín is the largest vineyard department in Argentina, about 25,800 ha in 2024 (INV), the heart of the Eastern Mendoza oasis along the Mendoza and Tunuyán rivers at 650 to 750 m. Hot, flat and fertile, it produces much of Argentina's everyday wine, grape juice and concentrate, with Criolla Grande, Cereza, Bonarda and Pedro Giménez.

ar-san-martin-2.name: San Martín (San Juan)
ar-san-martin-2.summary: San Martín in San Juan, east of the capital in the Tulum valley, has about 3,600 ha of vines (INV 2024). Not to be confused with Mendoza's much larger San Martín.

ar-san-pablo.name: San Pablo
ar-san-pablo.summary: San Pablo, recognised in 2019, is Uco's highest IG, a cold alluvial terrace in Tunuyán at roughly 1,300 to 1,700 m, where frost and snow are real risks. Its limits were drawn by geology and climate rather than politics. Wines are taut and aromatic: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Malbec with very high acidity. Salentein and Zuccardi are among the growers.

ar-san-rafael.name: San Rafael
ar-san-rafael.summary:
San Rafael is Mendoza's southern oasis, an irrigated plain at 450 to 800 m on the Diamante and Atuel rivers, about 230 km south of the city, with about 11,500 ha of vines (INV 2024). French, Italian and Spanish immigrants built it into a fruit-and-wine district from the late 19th century; the Bianchi, Suter and Goyenechea houses are long-standing names. It became Argentina's second DOC in 2007, though the denomination is little used.

San Rafael is cooler than eastern Mendoza thanks to its southern latitude, and its wines are fresh, fruity and fairly priced: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chenin Blanc and sparkling wines. The Cañón del Atuel and the 'Valle Grande' reservoir make it a tourism hub as well.

ar-san-rafael-2.name: San Rafael (IG)
ar-san-rafael-2.summary: The department of San Rafael is also registered as a plain IG with the same limits as the DOC; producers usually label this simpler designation.

ar-sanagasta.name: Sanagasta
ar-sanagasta.summary: Sanagasta, a hill valley north of La Rioja city, has a small wine tradition and a few hectares of Malbec.

ar-santa-lucia.name: Santa Lucía
ar-santa-lucia.summary: Santa Lucía, east of San Juan city, has about 900 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly traditional.

ar-santa-maria.name: Santa María
ar-santa-maria.summary: Santa María, in the north of Catamarca at about 1,900 m, is the southern end of the Calchaquí valleys system, with about 220 ha of Malbec and old Torrontés vines (INV 2024).

ar-santa-rosa.name: Santa Rosa
ar-santa-rosa.summary: Santa Rosa, at the south-eastern edge of the Eastern oasis along the Tunuyán river, has about 7,900 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly for everyday wine.

ar-sarmiento.name: Sarmiento
ar-sarmiento.summary: Sarmiento, in southern San Juan, is the province's leading Malbec department (932 ha of Malbec of about 7,000 ha of vines, INV 2024) and contains the high Pedernal valley.

ar-sarmiento-2.name: Sarmiento (Chubut)
ar-sarmiento-2.summary: Sarmiento, in central Chubut near lakes Musters and Colhué Huapi at about 45.5°S, is one of the southernmost wine IGs in the world, recognised in 2023. Small vineyards of cool-climate varieties grow in a cold, windy steppe oasis.

ar-sorocayense.name: Sorocayense
ar-sorocayense.summary: Sorocayense (Paraje Sorocayense) is a locality in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG together with Tamberías and Hilario in 2024.

ar-tafi.name: Tafí
ar-tafi.summary: Tafí (Tafí del Valle department) is Tucumán's wine IG, taking in Colalao del Valle and Amaicha del Valle on the Calchaquí side of the Aconquija range at about 1,700 to 2,000 m, where Malbec and Torrontés grow. Amaicha's indigenous community runs its own community winery, Los Amaichas.

ar-tamberias.name: Tamberías
ar-tamberias.summary: Tamberías is a village at about 1,500 m in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG at the request of the Calingasta municipality, together with Hilario and Sorocayense. Its name refers to Inca *tambos* (waystations) on the trail along the valley.

ar-tandil.name: Tandil
ar-tandil.summary: Tandil, in the granite hills of the Tandilia system, became an IG in July 2024, the third in the Buenos Aires hills. Better known for salami and cheese, it now has a few vineyards on rocky slopes.

ar-tinogasta.name: Tinogasta
ar-tinogasta.summary: Tinogasta, around Fiambalá and Tinogasta towns in western Catamarca at 1,200 to 1,700 m, is the province's main wine area, with old Torrontés and Criolla vines, adobe wineries and home-made *vino patero*, plus modern altitude Syrah and Malbec.

ar-trevelin.name: Trevelin
ar-trevelin.summary: Trevelin, a town founded by Welsh settlers in the Andean foothills of Chubut at about 43°S, became an IG in 2020. Vineyards near the Futaleufú river, among the southernmost in the Americas, grow Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling for crisp, low-alcohol wines.

ar-tucuman.name: Tucumán
ar-tucuman.summary: Tucumán's provincial IG covers a small wine area of about 145 ha (INV 2024), almost all in the Tafí del Valle department on the Calchaquí side of the mountains, at Colalao del Valle and Amaicha del Valle, where Malbec and Torrontés grow at about 1,700 to 2,000 m.

ar-tunuyan.name: Tunuyán
ar-tunuyan.summary: Tunuyán is the central Uco department, about 10,200 ha of vines (INV 2024), from the Tunuyán river plain to the Andean foothills. It contains the IGs of Los Chacayes, Vista Flores and San Pablo, and the area of Los Árboles, where Bodegas Salentein built its cross-shaped winery at the end of the 1990s.

ar-tupungato.name: Tupungato
ar-tupungato.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Valle de Tupungato 2006)
ar-tupungato.summary: Tupungato is the northernmost Uco department, named after the 6,570-m Tupungato volcano that looms over it. About 10,600 ha of vines (INV 2024) climb from 900 m to over 1,500 m in Gualtallary. Chandon, in Argentina since 1959, was an early investor here for sparkling base wine; Catena's Adrianna vineyard (1992) showed that the high north-west could make world-class Malbec and Chardonnay.

ar-ullum.name: Ullum
ar-ullum.summary: Ullum, west of San Juan city around the Ullum reservoir, has about 1,200 ha of vines (INV 2024) on stony soils in the pre-cordillera.

ar-valle-de-chanarmuyo.name: Valle de Chañarmuyo
ar-valle-de-chanarmuyo.summary: Chañarmuyo is a high valley at about 1,700 m in Famatina department where Bodega Chañarmuyo planted a modern estate in the 2000s. Recognised in 2014, it gives altitude Malbec, Cabernet and Torrontés of more freshness than the lower Famatina floor.

ar-valle-de-pucara.name: Valle de Pucará
ar-valle-de-pucara.summary: Valle de Pucará, recognised in March 2025 at the request of Finca de los Viñedos Imposibles, is a high side valley west of Angastaco in San Carlos department, at well over 2,000 m. Its name (from the Quechua for 'fortress') recalls pre-Hispanic hilltop sites; local growers make Malbec and Criolla of extreme concentration.

ar-valle-de-uco.name: Valle de Uco
ar-valle-de-uco.grapes: Malbec (16,584 ha across its three departments in 2024), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
ar-valle-de-uco.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Andes with river stones, sand and calcium carbonate crusts; 900 to 1,600 m; cool continental climate, about 300 mm of summer rain, frequent hail and spring frost.
ar-valle-de-uco.nerd_note: The three Uco departments together hold 41.6% of all Malbec in Mendoza (INV 2025).
ar-valle-de-uco.summary:
The Uco Valley is where Argentine wine went uphill and found its future. It is a long depression at 900 to 1,600 m between the Andes and a low pre-cordillera, 80 to 120 km south-west of Mendoza city, covering the departments of Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos and watered by the Tunuyán river and Andean streams. Historically it grew fruit, potatoes and some Criolla; the turn came in the 1990s, when Nicolás Catena planted the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary (1992) and a wave of French, Dutch and Argentine investors followed: Clos de los Siete, Salentein, Andeluna, O. Fournier, and later Zuccardi's winery at Paraje Altamira.

The valley's soils are alluvial fans pushed out from the Andes: stony and often calcareous near the mountains, with sand and silt further east. Each fan and each terrace behaves differently, so Uco has spawned more district IGs than anywhere else in Argentina (Los Chacayes, Paraje Altamira, San Pablo, Pampa El Cepillo, Vista Flores, La Consulta, El Peral, Cordón del Cepillo, with Gualtallary pending), and producers increasingly label single 'parajes'. The climate is cool for Argentina, with frost and hail as real threats.

Uco Malbec is fresher and more floral than Luján's, with violet, red fruit, firm chalky tannins and high natural acidity; Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir excel too. Valle de Uco is by far Argentina's most used IG: 41% of all IG wine sold in 2022 and 45% of IG exports (INV).

ar-valle-de-zonda.name: Valle de Zonda
ar-valle-de-zonda.summary: Valle de Zonda, recognised in 2015, is a narrower IG for the vineyards of the Zonda valley itself, a pre-cordillera basin west of San Juan city where cooler nights and stony soils give fresher reds than the Tulum oasis.

ar-valle-del-pedernal.name: Valle del Pedernal
ar-valle-del-pedernal.summary: Pedernal is San Juan's high-altitude showcase: a narrow valley at about 1,250 to 1,500 m in Sarmiento department, between pre-cordillera ranges, where calcareous, stony soils and cold nights produce Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Chardonnay with real freshness. Pyros and Viñas de Segisa are among its producers.

ar-valle-del-tulum.name: Valle del Tulum
ar-valle-del-tulum.summary: The Tulum valley is the central irrigated oasis of San Juan around the provincial capital, at 600 to 700 m along the San Juan river. Hot and sunny with under 100 mm of rain, it grows most of the province's grapes: Cereza, Criolla, Pedro Giménez and Moscatel for wine, juice and raisins, alongside Syrah, Malbec and Bonarda for fine wine. Departments such as Pocito, Rawson, Caucete, 25 de Mayo, Sarmiento and San Martín lie within it.

ar-valle-fertil.name: Valle Fértil
ar-valle-fertil.summary: Valle Fértil, in the eastern San Juan hills, is a green valley with almost no vineyard today; its IG dates from the 2002 national list.

ar-valles-calchaquies.name: Valles Calchaquíes
ar-valles-calchaquies.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica
ar-valles-calchaquies.terroir: Sandy and gravelly alluvium on valley terraces, granite and schist slopes; 1,700 to 3,100 m; high UV, cold nights, under 200 mm of rain.
ar-valles-calchaquies.summary:
The Calchaquí valleys form one of the highest wine regions on Earth: a 270-km chain of arid valleys along the Calchaquí river and its tributaries, crossing Salta, Tucumán and Catamarca from Cachi and Payogasta in the north to Cafayate and Santa María in the south. Vineyards sit between about 1,700 m at Cafayate and over 3,000 m around Payogasta, under the Andes' eastern ranges. The Jesuits and Spanish settlers brought Criolla vines in the colonial era; the Isasmendi and Dávalos families planted French Malbec and Cabernet at Colomé in the 1850s.

Altitude defines the wine. Strong ultraviolet light thickens grape skins, giving Malbec, Tannat and Cabernet Sauvignon deep colour and firm tannin; nights are cold, so acidity stays high. Torrontés Riojano reaches its most perfumed and best-balanced style at Cafayate. Soils are sandy and stony alluvium with low organic matter, and rainfall is under 200 mm. The IG was the fourth most used Argentine IG in 2022 (INV).

ar-valles-del-famatina.name: Valles del Famatina
ar-valles-del-famatina.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
ar-valles-del-famatina.summary: The Famatina valleys, between the Famatina range (6,100 m) and the Velasco hills in La Rioja, are the province's wine heartland, with Chilecito at the centre at about 1,000 to 1,400 m. This is the home of Torrontés Riojano, grown for generations on high pergolas and made into aromatic, floral whites, and of the giant La Riojana cooperative. Valles del Famatina was Argentina's third most used IG in 2022 and second for exports by volume (INV), mostly as good-value Torrontés and Malbec.

ar-valles-templados.name: Valles Templados
ar-valles-templados.summary: Valles Templados ('temperate valleys'), recognised in August 2025 at the request of Jujuy's provincial government, covers the lower, greener valleys of Jujuy around San Salvador, El Carmen and Perico, where a subtropical-montane climate allows a small but growing wine production.

ar-victoria-entre-rios.name: Victoria, Entre Ríos
ar-victoria-entre-rios.summary: Victoria, on the Paraná river delta in Entre Ríos, revives a wine tradition that flourished in the province in the late 19th and early 20th centuries before 1930s national regulation favoured Cuyo and many vineyards were uprooted. Recognised in 2021, it grows small volumes of red wine in a humid, temperate climate.

ar-villa-ventana.name: Villa Ventana
ar-villa-ventana.summary: Villa Ventana, in the Sierra de la Ventana hills of south-western Buenos Aires province, was recognised in 2011. A handful of small wineries grow cool-climate varieties on stony slopes.

ar-vinchina.name: Vinchina
ar-vinchina.summary: Vinchina, in the far west of La Rioja near the Andes, is a high, arid department with tiny vineyards for local wine.

ar-vista-flores.name: Vista Flores
ar-vista-flores.summary: Vista Flores is the Tunuyán district around which Michel Rolland and partners created Clos de los Siete from 1998: a block of about 850 ha divided among several wineries (Monteviejo, Cuvelier, DiamAndes, Rolland), each making its own wine and contributing to the shared Clos de los Siete blend. At about 1,000 to 1,200 m, sandy-loam and stony soils give plush, polished Malbec.

ar-vistalba.name: Vistalba
ar-vistalba.summary: Vistalba, a small district at about 1,000 m beside Las Compuertas on the north bank of the Mendoza river, was recognised as an IG in 2022. Old Malbec on stony soils gives refined, perfumed wines; Carlos Pulenta's Vistalba estate and Fabre Montmayou are based here.

ar-zonda.name: Zonda
ar-zonda.summary: Zonda is the department west of San Juan city, in a valley between pre-cordillera ranges that gave its name to the Zonda wind. About 1,000 ha of vines (INV 2024) with a reputation for fresher Syrah and Malbec.

sites.name: Bodega Catena Zapata
sites.text: The Catena family's pyramid in Agrelo, built in the late 1990s to a Mayan-inspired design by Pablo Sánchez Elía, overlooks the La Pirámide vineyard planted in 1983. Nicolás Catena's research on high-altitude Malbec, continued by his daughter Laura's Catena Institute of Wine, transformed Argentina's image. Named World's Best Vineyard in 2023.

sites.name: Adrianna Vineyard, Gualtallary
sites.text: Planted by Nicolás Catena in 1992 at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary, Tupungato, where locals said grapes would never ripen. Its parcels on calcareous gravels give the Adrianna Malbecs (Mundus Bacillus Terrae, Fortuna Terrae, River Stones) and the White Bones and White Stones Chardonnays, among the most acclaimed wines of South America.

sites.name: Achával-Ferrer
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by Santiago Achával and Manuel Ferrer with Italian winemaker Roberto Cipresso among the partners, Achával-Ferrer helped prove that old, low-yielding Malbec vineyards could each make a distinct single-vineyard wine: Finca Altamira, Finca Bella Vista and Finca Mirador. Its winery stands by the Mendoza river in Perdriel.

sites.name: Zuccardi Valle de Uco
sites.text: Opened in 2016 at Paraje Altamira, the Zuccardi winery is built from the rounded, lime-coated stones of its own vineyards, and works largely with concrete fermenters and untoasted casks. Sebastián Zuccardi's parcel-by-parcel approach made it the World's Best Vineyard in 2019, 2020 and 2021.

sites.name: Finca Piedra Infinita
sites.text: Zuccardi's estate vineyard at Paraje Altamira, named for the 'infinite stone' of its soils: river cobbles coated in calcium carbonate over sand. Its Malbecs, including Finca Piedra Infinita and Gravascal, are made by soil type rather than variety.

sites.name: Bodega Noemía
sites.text: Founded in 2001 in Mainqué, Río Negro, by Italian Countess Noemi Marone Cinzano and Danish winemaker Hans Vinding-Diers, around a Malbec vineyard planted in 1932. Biodynamically farmed, flood-irrigated old vines in the Patagonian wind give some of Argentina's most perfumed Malbec.

sites.name: Bodega Chacra
sites.text: Piero Incisa della Rocchetta, of the family behind Sassicaia, founded Chacra in Mainqué in 2004 around ungrafted Pinot Noir planted in 1932 and 1955, naming wines after the planting years (Treinta y Dos, Cincuenta y Cinco). Biodynamic farming and Burgundian restraint made it Patagonia's reference for Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Bodega Humberto Canale
sites.text: Founded in 1909 by engineer Humberto Canale near General Roca, the pioneer winery of Patagonia. Still family-owned, it keeps old Semillon, Malbec and Merlot vineyards in the Alto Valle among apple and pear orchards.

sites.name: Bodega Colomé
sites.text: Founded in 1831 by the governor of Salta, Nicolás Severo de Isasmendi, Colomé is one of Argentina's oldest working wineries; French Malbec and Cabernet were brought in 1854. Swiss collector Donald Hess bought it in 2001, planted vineyards from 2,300 to 3,111 m and opened a James Turrell museum on the estate.

sites.name: Altura Máxima vineyard
sites.text: Colomé's vineyard at 3,111 m near Payogasta in the upper Calchaquí valley, among the highest commercial vineyards in the world. Frost, wind and extreme ultraviolet light make yields tiny; the Malbec and Pinot Noir sold as Altura Máxima are deeply coloured yet fresh.

sites.name: El Esteco, Cafayate
sites.text: A winery founded in 1892 by the Michel brothers at the edge of Cafayate, long known as Michel Torino. Today El Esteco keeps old Torrontés and Criolla vines, makes the Old Vines range, and its colonial estate houses the Patios de Cafayate hotel.

sites.name: Bodega Weinert
sites.text: Bernardo Weinert, born in Brazil, founded the winery in 1975 in a late 19th-century cellar in Carrodilla, Luján de Cuyo. Weinert is famous for ageing reds for years in large, old oak casks, the Cavas de Weinert style, a living link to Argentina's pre-1990s tradition.

sites.name: Cheval des Andes
sites.text: A joint venture launched in 1999 by Château Cheval Blanc and Terrazas de los Andes, with its own winery in Las Compuertas. The blend of old-vine Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, flood-irrigated as in Mendoza tradition, is a Saint-Émilion view of the Andes.

sites.name: Terrazas de los Andes
sites.text: LVMH's Argentine still-wine house, founded in 1999 and housed in a restored late 19th-century winery in Perdriel. Its name refers to the vineyard 'terraces' at different altitudes chosen for each variety, a founding idea of the high-altitude movement.

sites.name: Bodega Chandon
sites.text: Moët & Chandon's first winery outside France, established in Argentina in 1959 in Agrelo. It built the country's sparkling-wine industry and planted early vineyards in the Uco Valley; the El Peral IG (2022) was granted at its request.

sites.name: Bodegas Salentein
sites.text: Dutch businessman Mijndert Pon founded Salentein in Los Árboles, Tunuyán, in the late 1990s. Its cross-shaped winery with a circular barrel cellar, the Killka art gallery and a chapel became icons of the Uco Valley boom; vineyards reach up to about 1,700 m in San Pablo.

sites.name: Clos de los Siete
sites.text: A block of about 850 ha on the western edge of Vista Flores, Tunuyán, bought from 1998 by Michel Rolland and French partners and shared among several wineries (Monteviejo, Cuvelier Los Andes, DiamAndes, Rolland). Each makes its own wines and contributes to the shared Clos de los Siete blend.

sites.name: Bodega Trapiche (Espejo de Trapiche)
sites.text: Trapiche, founded in 1883 and owned by governor Tiburcio Benegas, who pushed for the 1885 railway, is one of Argentina's founding wine brands. Its Florentine-style 1912 winery in Maipú, built beside the railway line with its own rail spur, was restored and reopened in 2008.

sites.name: Bodega Norton
sites.text: Founded in 1895 by the English engineer Edmund James Palmer Norton, who came to Argentina to build the Transandine railway. Owned since 1989 by the family of Austrian Gernot Langes-Swarovski, it farms large estates in Perdriel.

sites.name: Bodegas López
sites.text: Founded in 1898 by José López Rivas, a Spanish immigrant from Málaga, in Maipú. Still family-run, López keeps the traditional style of long ageing in huge old oak foudres, and its Château Vieux and Montchenot reds are released with years of bottle age.

sites.name: Club Tapiz
sites.text: A historic estate house of 1890 in Russell, Maipú, now an inn and restaurant belonging to the Tapiz group, which farms high vineyards in San Pablo in the Uco Valley.

sites.name: Bodega La Rural (Museo del Vino San Felipe)
sites.text: Founded in 1885 by Felipe Rutini, an immigrant from the Marche, at Coquimbito in Maipú. Its wine museum displays thousands of objects from Mendoza's past, from cowhide presses to early bottling machines; the Rutini brand now makes wine mostly from Tupungato.

sites.name: Museo Nacional del Vino y la Vendimia
sites.text: The national wine and harvest museum in Maipú, housed in the early 20th-century villa of Juan Giol, whose La Colina de Oro winery was once among the largest in the world. It tells the story of Mendoza's harvest festival and industrial wine age.

sites.name: Escorihuela Gascón
sites.text: Founded in 1884 by Spanish immigrant Miguel Escorihuela Gascón in Godoy Cruz, now inside the city. Its old cellars and park house the restaurant 1884, opened by chef Francis Mallmann.

sites.name: Bodega Lagarde
sites.text: Founded in 1897 in Mayor Drummond, Luján de Cuyo, Lagarde is one of Mendoza's oldest wineries still working in its original buildings, with old Malbec and an early Argentine planting of Viognier.

sites.name: Familia Schroeder
sites.text: A winery on the San Patricio del Chañar plateau in Neuquén. During its construction in the early 2000s workers found dinosaur fossils, later described as the titanosaur *Panamericansaurus schroederi* and displayed in the cellar; the winery's Saurus label celebrates them.

sites.name: Bodega del Fin del Mundo
sites.text: Planted from the late 1990s on desert plateau in San Patricio del Chañar, Neuquén, with water piped from the Neuquén river; one of the projects that put northern Patagonia on the wine map.

sites.name: Patagonian Wines (Weinert), El Hoyo
sites.text: Bernardo Weinert's estate in the pre-Andean valley of El Hoyo, Chubut, near El Bolsón at about 300 m and 42°S. Its roughly 28 ha of Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and Gewürztraminer led to the El Hoyo IG in 2023.

sites.name: Estancia Jesuítica de Caroya
sites.text: A 17th-century Jesuit estancia north of Córdoba that supplied the Jesuit college with food and wine until the order's expulsion in 1767. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba; its lands were later settled by Friulian vine growers in 1878.

sites.name: Área Fundacional, Mendoza
sites.text: The site of Mendoza's foundation by Pedro del Castillo in 1561, destroyed by the earthquake of 1861. A museum over the excavated ruins of the old cabildo shows the colonial city whose irrigation canals and vineyards began Argentine wine country.

sites.name: Quebrada de Humahuaca vineyards (Maimará)
sites.text: Terraced vineyards at 2,300 to over 2,500 m around Maimará and Tilcara in the UNESCO-listed Quebrada de Humahuaca, below the multicoloured hills of the Paleta del Pintor. Producers such as Fernando Dupont make intense Malbec, Cabernet Franc and Syrah.

sites.name: Costa & Pampa, Chapadmalal
sites.text: Trapiche's Atlantic experiment, a vineyard a few kilometres from the sea south of Mar del Plata, planted around 2010. Its Albariño, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, salty and taut, led to the Chapadmalal IG in 2014.
